passage: Himani, sit. I am Sarita, and you asked why I never fight with your Uncle Rohit over the house papers, so I'll tell you. When I was twenty-five, Amma and Baba bought Rohit a motorbike for passing one exam. My first-class degree got a sweet and a pat on the head. Then came the talk about the will, and Baba said, "Rohit will need more, he's a boy." I sat in the kitchen while my tea went cold, feeling like furniture. I could have shouted at Rohit. He hadn't asked for any of it. Instead, one evening I told Amma, quietly, "It hurts when my work goes unseen." She went silent, then said she hadn't realised. It didn't fix everything. But I stopped waiting for applause and took the evening course I'd wanted. Rohit and I still share Diwali dinners. That mattered more than winning an argument would have.

qa.q: What did Amma and Baba buy Rohit for passing one exam?
How did Sarita feel in the kitchen while the tea went cold?
qa.a: Sarita felt like furniture, unseen and hurt, yet did not blame Rohit, who hadn't asked for any of it.

qa.q: What did Sarita do instead of turning it into a fight with Rohit?
qa.a: Sarita told Amma quietly that it hurts when work goes unseen, took the evening course Sarita had wanted, and kept sharing Diwali dinners with Rohit.

qa.q: How might Amma have experienced Sarita's quiet words?
qa.a: Amma went silent and then said she hadn't realised, which suggests Amma had not noticed the hurt until it was said calmly.

grounding: An adult child feels unseen by parents who favour a sibling, says so calmly, avoids war with the sibling and builds worth through their own course.
